subject: Communication Skills I
text: backgrounding (c) silences Leisure in a capitalist society is a paradoxical concept. On the surface it promises freedom and relaxation, but in reality, it is often shaped and commodified by market forces. Capitalism encourages people to view leisure as something to consume, whether through vacations entertainment, or self-care products, rather than as a time for personal growth, reflection, or genuine rest. The constant drive for productivity means even leisure can feel like another task to optimize, turning hobbies or downtime into opportunities for self-improvement or side hustles. Moreover, leisure time is unequally distributed. The wealthy enjoy more time and means to pursue enriching activities, while those in lower-income brackets may find themselves with less time due to longer work hours or financial pressures. As a result, true leisure, free from market demands, becomes a privilege rather than a right. In this sense, capitalist society frames leisure not as a break from the economic system but as an extension of it. While there are undeniable benefits to having access to leisure activities and consumer-driven recreation, the deeper issue lies in how capitalism commodifies our time, turning even moments of rest into transactions. This calls into question whether leisure in a capitalist framework can ever be fully liberating. b. Write a response to the piece in Q 4 a.

subject: Communication Skills I
text: backgrounding (c) silences While climate change is undeniably a serious global crisis, the anxiety surrounding it is sometimes misplaced or misdirected. Many people feel overwhelmed by the sheer magnitude of the problem, often translating their concern into an obsessive focus on individual actions—like avoiding plastic straws or reducing personal carbon footprints. While personal responsibility is important, this intense focus on small changes can overshadow the need for large-scale, systemic solutions. The truth is, climate change is driven largely by industrial pollution deforestation, and government inaction. Large corporations and policies contribute significantly more to global emissions than individuals, yet much of the public discourse places the burden of solving climate change on personal choices. This misplaced anxiety can lead to feelings of guilt or powerlessness, as people question whether their efforts to recycle or cut back on energy use will ever make a real difference. However, this anxiety, while understandable, could be better directed toward advocating for systemic change—pushing governments and corporations to adopt more sustainable practices, invest in renewable energy, and enforce stricter environmental regulations. Collective action is far more effective than individual efforts in addressing the root causes of climate change. While it is important for individuals to contribute to the solution, it’s crucial to recognize that climate anxiety should inspire broader, more impactful actions rather than paralyze people with fear over their personal habits. In short, anxiety about climate change is valid, but its power lies in motivating organized, collective efforts that tackle the larger forces behind the crisis. b. subject: Communication Skills I
text: Is the following an instance of persuasion? Justify your answer Stimit works at an IT Firm. His senior to whom he reports - Amol meets him in the corridor at 6:30 pm – just as Stimit was leaving for home. Amol persuades Stimit to stay till late so that the project speeds up and is completed as per schedule. Amol framed the request as voluntary praising teamwork and mentioning possible future opportunities for those who contribute. While Amol didn’t explicitly say there would be consequences for refusing, Stimit felt an unspoken pressure to agree fearing that his refusal could negatively impact his standing in the team.
